newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Stan Chart Bank sees long-term future in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Stan Chart Bank sees long-term future in Hong Kong.

text.p: Standard Chartered Plc chief executive officer Malcolm Williamson said on Wednesday his bank had a long-term future in Hong Kong.

Responding to recent press comments suggesting the London-based bank might find it difficult to operate in the territory after it reverts to China this year, Williamson said such suggestions were absurd.

"The fact that we are a British bank doesn't mean anything," he told Reuters. "We are British in terms of our head office but with 70 percent of our business in Asia, we are actually more of an Asian bank."
"I absolutely do not subscribe to the view that with the change of government we will in some way be marginalised," he said in an interview.
Hong Kong will be handed back to China from Britain on the night of June 30, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
But Williamson said Standard Chartered, which has a major presence in Hong Kong and even issues its own bank notes there, expected its commitment to the territory to grow over time.

"As far as Hong Kong is concerned, we are a note issuing bank and indeed were asked by the Chinese to carry on being a note issuing bank after the handover to China, in common with Hong Kong Bank and Bank of China," he said.

"They have no plans to give the entire franchise to the Bank of China. The only thing we have to change are the actual notes themseves. We have to take the Queen's head off and have something that is rather more appropriate," he added.
"We have extremely good relations with China. I spend quite a lot of my time in Beijing. There is no reason which I can see why we can't be successful," he said.
Williamson said he expected Hong Kong to become a more competitive environment after the handover but said the bank could cope with that.

"We have a big business and we have lots of very satisfied customers. It seems to me that what will happen is that the market will be more competitive and the survivors will be people who give the customers what they want at a price they can afford," he said.

"We wouldn't be investing heavily in China if we weren't confident about the future. We have the biggest foreign bank branch network in China. We have just been included with Hong Kong Bank in the experiment in Pudong, in Shanghai of the renminbi. We have a licence for that. I can't think that if the Chinese were discriminating against the British banks that we would have obtained that licence.

"Another example of our cooperation with China is the fact that we are linked up with the Bank of China with an experiment with smart cards in China. It is hardly likely to happen if the barriers were up against us," he added.
